en: The Sūtra on Neither Increasing nor Decreasing, spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of North India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
Therein, he was together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, as well as immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have circled through the six realms and traveled back and forth within the three worlds; amidst the four modes of birth, they transmigrate through birth and death, experiencing endless suffering.
"Bhagavān! Does this assembly of sentient beings, this ocean of sentient beings, undergo increase or decrease?
Or is it without increase or decrease?"
"This meaning is profound and obscure; I have not yet been able to understand it.
If someone were to question me, how should I answer?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
“Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!

It is because you desire to bring peace and security to all sentient beings, to bring happiness to all sentient beings, out of compassion for all sentient beings, for the benefit of all sentient beings, and for the welfare, peace, and happiness of all sentient beings— including gods and humans— that you are able to ask me about this profound meaning.”
Śāriputra! If you had not asked the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha about such a matter, there would have been many faults. Why is this so?
In the present and future worlds, all sentient beings, including gods and humans, will long endure decline, affliction, and harm, and will forever lose all benefit and peace.
Śāriputra! That which is called great wrong view is the view that the realm of sentient beings increases or the view that the realm of sentient beings decreases. Śāriputra!

These sentient beings with such great wrong views, because of these views, are born blind and sightless; therefore, throughout the long night, they wander delusively upon false paths, and by reason of this, they fall into the various evil realms in the present life.

Śāriputra! What is called a great peril is this: the stubborn attachment and false clinging to the increase of the realm of sentient beings, and the stubborn attachment and false clinging to the decrease of the realm of sentient beings.

Śāriputra! These sentient beings are firmly attached to false attachments; therefore, throughout the long night, they falsely practice deviant paths. By reason of these causes and conditions, they will fall into the various evil realms in future lives.

“Śāriputra! Because all foolish ordinary beings do not know the single dharma-realm as it truly is, and do not see the single dharma-realm as it truly is, they give rise to a mind of false views, saying that the realm of sentient beings increases or that the realm of sentient beings decreases.”
Śāriputra! While the Tathāgata remains in the world, my disciples do not give rise to such views.

However, after my parinirvāṇa, when more than five hundred years have passed, there will be many sentient beings who are foolish and lack wisdom; though they shave their hair and beards, don the three dharma robes, and manifest the appearance of śramaṇas within the Buddha-dharma, they will lack the virtuous conduct of a śramaṇa within.
People such as these are not truly śramaṇas though they call themselves śramaṇas, nor are they disciples of the Buddha though they claim to be disciples of the Buddha; yet they say of themselves:
"I am a śramaṇa, a true disciple of the Buddha."
"Such persons as these give rise to views of increase and decrease.
Why is this? Because these sentient beings rely upon the Tathāgata’s sutras of provisional meaning, lack the eye of wisdom, and are far removed [from the truth]."
Because they hold a view of emptiness that is not in accordance with reality, they do not know in accordance with reality the initial resolve realized by the Tathāgata;
they do not know in accordance with reality the cultivation and accumulation of the immeasurable meritorious practices of enlightenment;
they do not know in accordance with reality the immeasurable dharmas attained by the Tathāgata; they do not know in accordance with reality the immeasurable powers of the Tathāgata... [and so forth].
Because they do not truly know the immeasurable realm of the Tathāgata; because they do not have faith in the immeasurable sphere of activity of the Tathāgata;
because they do not know, as it really is, the inconceivable and immeasurable mastery over dharmas of the Tathāgata;

because they do not know, as it really is, the inconceivable and immeasurable skillful means of the Tathāgata; and because they are unable to correctly discern the immeasurable [qualities] of the Tathāgata...
Because they take the distinctions of measure as their objective domain, they are unable to skillfully enter the inconceivable great compassion of the Tathāgata,
and they do not know the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata as it truly is.

“Śāriputra! Because foolish worldlings lack the wisdom born of hearing, when they hear of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, they give rise to views of annihilation and views of extinction. Because they give rise to conceptions of annihilation and extinction, they claim that the realm of sentient beings diminishes; thus they commit a great false view, an extremely grave and evil karma.”

Furthermore, Śāriputra, these sentient beings, relying upon the view of diminution, further give rise to three views; these three types of views are inseparable from that view of diminution, just like a net.
What are the three views?
First is the view of annihilationism, which means that things are ultimately exhausted;
second is the view of extinction, which means that this itself is nirvāṇa.
Third is the view of non-nirvāṇa, which means that this nirvāṇa is ultimately empty and quiescent.
Śāriputra, these three kinds of views are bound in this way, grasped in this way, and contacted in this way.
Due to the causal conditions of these three views, two further types of false views arise in succession; these two views are inseparable from those three, like a net.
What are the two views?
First, the view of desirelessness; second, the view that there is ultimately no nirvana. "Śāriputra!
Based on the view of non-desire, two further views arise; these two types of views are inseparable from the view of non-desire, like a net.
What are these two views?
The first is the view of clinging to precepts and rituals; the second is the perverted view that conceives of purity within the impure.

"Śāriputra, based on the view of the ultimate non-existence of nirvāṇa, six further kinds of views arise; these six kinds of views are inseparable from the view of the non-existence of nirvāṇa, just like the meshes of a net."

What are the six views? First, the view that the world has a beginning; second, the view that the world has an end; third, the view that sentient beings are created by illusion; fourth, the view that there is neither suffering nor pleasure; fifth, the view that there are no sentient beings; and sixth, the view that there are no noble truths.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, these sentient beings, relying upon views of increase, further give rise to two other views; these two kinds of views are inseparable from that view of increase, just like a net."
What are the two views?
The first is the view that Nirvāṇa arises for the first time; the second is the view that it exists suddenly, without cause and without condition. Śāriputra!
These two kinds of views cause sentient beings to lack the mind of aspiration and the mind of diligent effort toward wholesome dharmas.

Śāriputra, because these sentient beings have given rise to these two kinds of views, even if the seven Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas were to appear in succession in the world to preach the Dharma for them, it would be impossible for them to develop a mind of aspiration or a mind of diligent effort toward wholesome dharmas.

“Śāriputra! These two kinds of views are the very root of ignorance and all delusions; namely, the view that nirvāṇa arises for the first time, and the view that it exists suddenly without cause or condition.”
“Śāriputra! These two kinds of views are the most evil roots and the gravest afflictions. Śāriputra!”
Based on these two views, all views arise; these all views are inseparable from those two views, like a net.
As for "all views," this refers to various kinds of views—whether internal or external, coarse or subtle, or intermediate.
“Śāriputra, what are called the view of increase and the view of decrease—these two views rely upon a single realm; they are one realm and are unified within that single realm.

Because all foolish worldlings do not know that single realm as it truly is, and do not see that single realm as it truly is, they give rise to an extremely evil mind of great false views, claiming that the realm of sentient beings increases or that the realm of sentient beings decreases.”
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What is this single realm?"

It is said that all foolish ordinary persons, because they do not know that single realm as it truly is and do not see that single realm as it truly is, give rise to an extremely evil and great mind of false view, claiming that the realm of sentient beings increases or that the realm of sentient beings decreases.
Śāriputra said: “Excellent, World-Honored One!
This meaning is extremely profound; I am unable to understand it.”
“I only pray that the Tathāgata will explain this for me, so that I may attain understanding.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra:
“This profound meaning is the realm of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and the sphere of activity of the Tathāgata’s mind.”
Śāriputra! Such profound meaning cannot be known, seen, or scrutinized by the wisdom of any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha; how much less could any ignorant ordinary person be able to fathom it?
Only the wisdom of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is able to observe and know this meaning. Śāriputra!
All the wisdom possessed by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can only be accepted through reverent faith regarding this meaning; they cannot know, see, or observe it as it truly is.

Śāriputra! That which is the profound meaning is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya); that which is the ultimate truth is the realm of sentient beings (sattva-dhātu); that which is the realm of sentient beings is the Tathāgatagarbha; and that which is the Tathāgatagarbha is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).

Śāriputra! As I have explained the meaning of the Dharma-body, it transcends the sands of the Ganges; it is inseparable from, not detached from, uninterrupted, and non-different from the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas—the merits and wisdom of the Tathāgata.
“Śāriputra! Just as a worldly lamp, its luminous color and tactile quality are neither separate nor detached from it;
and just as a mani jewel, its luminous color and form are neither separate nor detached from it.”

Śāriputra, the meaning of the Dharma-body as taught by the Tathāgata is likewise thus: it exceeds the sands of the Ganges, being inseparable from and non-detached from, uninterrupted and non-different from, the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas—the merits and wisdom of the Tathāgata.
“Śāriputra! This dharmakāya is a phenomenon that is neither born nor extinguished; it belongs neither to the past limit nor to the future limit, for it is free from the two extremes.”
Śāriputra! That which is not the past limit is because it is free from the time of arising; that which is not the future limit is because it is free from the time of cessation. Śāriputra!
The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is eternal, because it is a non-differentiating dharma and because it is an inexhaustible dharma. Śāriputra,
the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is constant, because it is a refuge that can always be relied upon and because it is equal throughout the limits of the future.
Śāriputra, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is cool and refreshing because it is the non-dual dharma and because it is the non-conceptualizing dharma.
Śāriputra, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is unchanging because it is not a dharma subject to extinction and because it is not a conditioned dharma.

“Śāriputra! This very dharmakāya, when enveloped by boundless afflictions exceeding the sands of the Ganges, following along with the world from beginningless time, drifting like waves and wandering through birth and death, is called a ‘sentient being.’”

Śāriputra! This very dharmakāya, having become weary of and detached from the suffering and affliction of worldly birth and death, having renounced all desires for existence, practicing the ten pāramitās, encompassing the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates, and cultivating the conduct of bodhi—this is called a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, this very dharmakāya is free from all worldly afflictions (*kleśa*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and fetters (*paryavasthāna*), and has transcended all suffering.

Being free from the stains of all afflictions, it attains purity and complete purification; it abides in the pure dharma on the other shore, reaches the ground of the aspirations of all sentient beings, and attains ultimate penetration into all spheres of experience, such that there is nothing superior to it."
Being free from all obscurations and free from all hindrances, having attained sovereign power over all phenomena, he is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Therefore, Śāriputra, there is no dharma-body apart from the realm of sentient beings, and there is no realm of sentient beings apart from the dharma-body;
the realm of sentient beings is itself the dharma-body, and the dharma-body is itself the realm of sentient beings.
Śāriputra! These two dharmas have the same meaning but different names.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
As I have explained above, within the realm of sentient beings there are likewise three kinds of dharmas, all of which are truly suchness (tathatā), neither different nor divergent.
What are these three dharmas?

First, the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha that is associated with the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), together with its pure dharmas; second, the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha that is dissociated from the primordial limit, together with its impure dharmas of entanglement by afflictions (*kleśa*); and third, the Tathāgatagarbha that is equal and constant throughout the future limit, together with its existent dharmas.

“Śāriputra, you should know that the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is associated with the primordial limit and consists of pure dharmas, is a reality that is non-false and non-delusory. It is inseparable from and not detached from the purity of wisdom; it is True Suchness (tathatā), the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and the inconceivable dharma. Since the beginningless primordial limit, this essence of the dharma associated with purity has existed.”
Śāriputra, based on this pure *tathatā* and *dharmadhātu*, for the sake of sentient beings, I speak of it as the inconceivable mind of intrinsic purity.

“Śāriputra, you should know that regarding the Tathāgatagarbha’s essence which has been dissociated from beginningless time, as well as the impure dharmas of the entanglements of afflictions—these impure dharmas, which have been dissociated from and entangled by afflictions since beginningless time, can only be severed by the Tathāgata’s wisdom of enlightenment.”

Śāriputra! Based on this inconceivable dharma-realm, which is enveloped by these afflictions yet remains dissociated from them, I have taught for the sake of sentient beings that the intrinsically pure mind is an inconceivable dharma defiled by adventitious afflictions.

“Śāriputra, you should know that the Tathāgatagarbha—which is equal throughout the future limit and possesses all phenomena—is the root of all dharmas. It encompasses all dharmas and is endowed with all dharmas; within the worldly dharmas, it does not depart from nor is it detached from the reality of all dharmas. It sustains all dharmas and gathers in all dharmas.”
Śāriputra! Based on this unborn and unceasing, eternally constant and cool, unchanging refuge, the inconceivable and pure *dharmadhātu*, I designate the name "sentient beings."

Why is this so? That which is called "sentient beings" is merely another name for the unborn and undying, the eternally constant and cool, the unchanging refuge, and the inconceivable, pure *dharmadhātu*. For this reason, I rely upon that Dharma and designate it by the name "sentient beings."
“Śāriputra! These three kinds of dharmas are all truly suchness (tathatā), neither different nor divergent.
Within these dharmas that are truly suchness, neither different nor divergent, one ultimately does not give rise to the two kinds of extremely evil and unwholesome false views.”
Why is this? Because they see according to reality.
That is to say, the view of diminution and the view of augmentation—Śāriputra!
"These two wrong views are utterly abandoned by all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and are censured by all Buddhas, Tathāgatas. Śāriputra!"

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who give rise to one view or two views, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are not their World-Honored Ones; such persons as these are not my disciples.

Śāriputra! Because these people have given rise to the causes and conditions of dualistic views, they pass from darkness into darkness and from obscurity into obscurity; I declare that such as these are called icchantikas.
Therefore, Śāriputra!
You should now train in this Dharma, transform those sentient beings, and cause them to leave behind the two views and abide within the Path of Righteousness. Śāriputra!
"You should also study such dharmas as these; abandon those two views and abide within the true path.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Śāriputra, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and the entire great assembly—including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others—all rejoiced greatly, and with faith and acceptance, they practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on Neither Increasing nor Decreasing Spoken by the Buddha
